title: Hash tables and collisions
summary: Place keys into a small hash table, handle two keys that choose the same slot, and find the right value by checking the stored key.
introduction: Imagine four trays for number cards. A quick rule chooses a tray for each card. Sometimes two cards choose the same tray, so we need a fair backup plan instead of throwing one away.
learningObjectives: Follow linear probing when two keys clash
Bound a search so a full table cannot loop forever

blocks.text: A **hash table** keeps keys in an array of slots. A **hash function** turns a key into a starting slot. Our tiny rule uses key % 4: the remainder after division by 4.
Both 5 % 4 and 9 % 4 are 1. Different keys choosing the same starting slot cause a **collision**. Equal hash results do not mean equal keys.
**Linear probing** solves this by trying the next slot, then the next. After slot 3, we wrap back to slot 0. We store the key along with its value, so a lookup can tell keys apart.

items: Start with four empty slots, numbered 0 to 3. A used flag says whether a slot holds a pair.
Insert key 5 with value 20. Its starting slot is 1, which is empty.
Insert key 9 with value 40. Slot 1 holds key 5, so put key 9 in slot 2.
Look up 9 from slot 1. Skip key 5, match key 9 in slot 2, and print 40.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

Use a separate local C11 compiler. Save this complete program as main.c; see Language setup.
Use a separate local C++17 compiler. Save this complete program as main.cpp; see Language setup.

variants.code:
keys = [0] * 4
values = [0] * 4
used = [False] * 4
inputs = [5, 9]
amounts = [20, 40]
for i in range(len(inputs)):
    for step in range(4):
        slot = (inputs[i] % 4 + step) % 4
        if not used[slot] or keys[slot] == inputs[i]:
            used[slot] = True
            keys[slot] = inputs[i]
            values[slot] = amounts[i]
            break
target = 9
for step in range(4):
    slot = (target % 4 + step) % 4
    if not used[slot]:
        break
    if keys[slot] == target:
        print(values[slot])
        break

blocks.text: The lookup repeats the same probing rule used for insertion. It compares actual keys before returning a value. The used flags let key 0 be a valid key; zero in an unused array cell is not treated as stored data.
Check the small and tricky cases

This tiny example accepts non-negative integer keys and inserts only two pairs into four slots. A full table needs an explicit failure result or a larger table. Our loops stop after four tries, so they cannot keep circling forever.

With no deletions, an unused slot tells lookup that the key is absent. Deletion needs special care: clearing an earlier slot could hide a later collided key. Real implementations use a special deleted marker or rebuild the cluster.

Hash tables can give O(1) average lookup with a suitable hash function and enough empty space. Many collisions can cause O(n) worst-case work. This tiny remainder rule is for learning, not a general-purpose hash function.

items: Change target from 9 to 5. Leave the stored pairs unchanged.
The output becomes 20. The lookup finds key 5 in its first slot, so it does not need the next slot.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not overwrite slot 1 just because key 9 hashes there. That would lose key 5. Compare keys and handle collisions.
